tmpl.reply:
Hello! To answer your question directly from the search records, the passages mention a few specific individuals connected to Badas̱ht: Ṭáhirih (also referred to as Qurratu'l 'Ayn in a memoir), Bahá’u’lláh, Quddús (or Goddous), and Munírih Khánum's uncle, Mírzá Hádí, who traveled there in company with about twenty-five other men ([*Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/munirih-khanum_memoirs-of-life-with-abdul-baha), Munírih Khánum). The texts note that "Daily contingents of the believers from different parts of Persia arrived, and joined the others until all had co" ([Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá](https://bahai-library.com/khanum_episodes_life)) (*Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, Munírih Khánum), but they do not list every individual participant by name.

To be precise about our sources and how they are classified in the study of this tradition:
- **Revealed Scripture** includes the primary writings of the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá.
- **Authorized Interpretation** consists of the authenticated writings and spoken words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi, which explain scripture without adding new laws.
- **Universal House of Justice Guidance** carries legal and administrative authority for the worldwide community, directing its plans and current administration rather than interpreting doctrinal texts.
- **Official Exposition, History, and Scholarship**—such as memoirs like those of Munírih Khánum ([Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá](https://bahai-library.com/khanum_episodes_life)), historical accounts, and scholarly works—provide eyewitness details, chronologies, and context, but do not set doctrine or interpretation. 
- **Community Practice** represents how believers apply these teachings in daily life, and **my own synthesis** is simply my way of gathering these points for you; neither should ever be mistaken for scripture or official doctrine.

Here is a short bullet list of the individuals explicitly named in connection with the gathering at Badas̱ht across this search's passages. Please note that this list may be incomplete, as the texts do not name every participant:

- Ṭáhirih (Qurratu'l 'Ayn) — mentioned as arriving with believers and being in Badas̱ht ([*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20901), ‘Abdu’l-Bahá; *Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, Munírih Khánum).
- Bahá’u’lláh — mentioned as going to Badas̱ht and being present there (*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá; *Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, Munírih Khánum).
- Quddús (Goddous) — mentioned as returning from Ḵhurasán and coming to Badas̱ht (*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá; *Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, Munírih Khánum).
- Mírzá Hádí — mentioned as Munírih Khánum's uncle who joined the company traveling to the Plain of Badasht (*Memoirs of Life with 'Abdu'l-Bahá*, Munírih Khánum).

I hope this helps with your student research as you continue exploring these histories. Warmly, Anís

results.text: What is the best prayer for guidance?

tmpl.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a quiet and beautiful question to bring to the threshold of prayer. When we look across the sacred traditions, what we call the "best" prayer for guidance is rarely a formula or a single fixed phrase; rather, it is the honest turning of the heart toward the Source of wisdom, asking to be aligned with a will higher than our own.

Looking to the revealed words themselves, different voices express this turning in their own profound ways. In the scriptures of Islám, we find the Prophet teaching the *Istikhara* prayer for any endeavor, where the seeker turns to divine knowledge: ['Allahumma inni astakhiruka bi’ilmika, Wa astaqdiruka bi-qudratika, Wa as'alaka min fadlika Al-‘azlm Fa-innaka taqdiru Wala aqdi'](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-al-bukhari/?paraId=para_2286&selectionString=a_i_al_bukhari_islam_ocean_en_1sy.0~a_i_al_bukhari_islam_ocean_en_1sy.1389) — [*Ṣaḥíḥ al-Bukhárí*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21075).

In the Bahá'í writings, the petition for guidance is equally an appeal to grace and ongoing mercy: ["Now that Thou hast guided them unto the door of Thy grace, O my Lord, cast them not away, by Thy bounty; and now that Thou hast summoned them unto the horizon of Thy Cause, keep them not back from Thee, by Thy graciousness and favor."](https://oceanlibrary.com/prayers-and-meditations-by-bahaullah/?paraId=para_429&selectionString=prayers_and_meditations_by_baha_u_llah_ocean_bahai0ab08b9a76883efd6ac65691b713a5a4_eo.0~prayers_and_meditations_by_baha_u_llah_ocean_bahai0ab08b9a76883efd6ac65691b713a5a4_eo.272) — [*Prayers and Meditations*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20805).

In the ancient Gathas of Zoroastrianism, the seeker asks the Creator to illuminate the path through righteousness: ["beseeching what in accordance with Your wished-for aim is best?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster/?paraId=para_259&selectionString=the-gathas_en_9x.0~the-gathas_en_9x.283) — [*The Gathas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21306).

And in the biblical Psalms, David simply prays to be instructed in the divine way: ["teach me thy statutes."](https://oceanlibrary.com/book-of-psalms-tehilim_david/?paraId=para_2229&selectionString=psalms-ot_en_1sm.0~psalms-ot_en_1sm.57) — [*The Bible (KJV), Psalms*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=912528).

Across all these varied expressions, what these texts share is a profound posture of humility—the recognition that true guidance comes not from self-assertion, but from surrendering one's steps to the care of the All-Knowing.

Warmly,  
Anís

While the primary Bahá’í writings do not provide a verse-by-verse commentary on the specific injunctions of the *Vendidad*—such as the laws surrounding the *nasu* (dead matter) or the construction of the *dakhma* (Tower of Silence)—they do address the station of Zoroaster as a divine Manifestation and trace the evolution of religious laws across successive dispensations.

Shoghi Effendi notes in [*God Passes By*](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_202&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_8d.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_8d.380) that the sacred books of Zoroastrianism pointed toward the advent of a future World-Saviour:

```bilingual
To His Dispensation the sacred books of the followers of Zoroaster had referred as that in which the sun must needs be brought to a standstill for no less than one whole month. <sup>1</sup>
To Him Zoroaster must have alluded when, according to tradition, He foretold that a period of three thousand years of conflict and contention must needs precede the advent of the World-Savior S̱háh-Bahrám, Who would triumph over Ahriman and usher in an era of blessedness and peace. <sup>2</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310) · <sup>2</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, *God Passes By*

### Cleanliness and Purity

**What the doctrine affirms:** The teachings emphasize both physical cleanliness and its spiritual counterpart, purity of heart and conduct. Bahá’u’lláh explains in the notes to [*The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307) that the Arabic word *liṭáfat* encompasses refinement, grace, cleanliness, and being sanctified and pure. The believers are exhorted to bathe regularly, wear clean clothes, and embody refinement.

**What it warns against:** The doctrine warns against reducing spiritual holiness to mere outward physical rituals or rigid material taboos disconnected from the inner state of the soul. While outward cleanliness is enjoined as a mark of civilization and respect, it is paired inextricably with upright character and the fear of God ([*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780)).

### Death and the Soul

**What the doctrine affirms:** Death is understood not as an end or a contamination, but as a normal stage in the soul's journey to the spiritual worlds. In [*Paris Talks*](https://oceanlibrary.com/paris-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_984&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_u3.0~abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_u3.381), ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of the soul's immortality and the illumination of the spirit:

```bilingual
Verily, the day is dawning when Paris will receive her illumination, and the Goodness and Mercy of God will be visible to every living creature. <sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation compiled from [*Paris Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20908)

**What it warns against:** The writings caution against fearing death as a state of annihilation or uncleanness, presenting it instead as a messenger of joy for the believer whose life has been oriented toward the divine. Furthermore, specific laws regarding the dead—such as the prohibition of cremation and the requirement for a specific burial ring and stone coffin—are set down directly in *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas* to govern the physical transition of the body with dignity, entirely superseding older customs of exposure or burning.

Anís

results.text: What is taqwah? I want to know about this virtue in Islam.

tmpl.reply:
Hello.

The term *taqwá* (تقوى), commonly translated as piety, fear of God, or God-consciousness, is rooted in an Arabic triliteral root associated with guarding, shielding, or protecting oneself. In the context of Islamic tradition, it signifies a state of vigilant moral and spiritual awareness—a protective shield one builds against heedlessness or wrongdoing through mindfulness of the Divine.

When looking across different layers of religious and intellectual life, this virtue is understood and discussed in distinct ways:

*   **Revealed Scripture and Tradition:** Within Islamic scripture and the Hadith, *taqwá* is presented as a foundational orientation of the heart, guiding human action toward righteousness and away from harm.
*   **Authorized Interpretation:** In various theological commentaries across traditions, terms of piety are often viewed not merely as passive fear, but as an active, conscious discipline of the self. For instance, in other writings influenced by Islamic terminology, such as the Persian and Arabic works of Bahá'u'lláh, terms like *taqiyyah* or related concepts of piety (*amánat* and *taqwá*) are enjoined upon believers as qualities that unlock security and exalt human character, as seen when He enjoins "on you honesty and piety" ([Epistle to the Son of the Wolf](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_46&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl40.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl40.318)) ([*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780), para. 46).

results.text: What do end times prophecies say about universal liberation?

tmpl.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a quiet joy to look into this with you. When we turn to the vast library of human memory and scripture to ask how different traditions speak of universal liberation, we find that the texts themselves do not present a single, uniform scenario of "end times" in the modern sense. Instead, they point to doors of emancipation that open through knowledge, realization, and divine grace.

To see how these traditions speak across their varied languages, it is illuminating to place an original line beside its translation. In the Sikh tradition, Guru Arjan Dev Ji writes of a liberation that extends outward to the entire cosmos:

> ਆਪਿ ਮੁਕਤੁ ਮੁਕਤੁ ਕਰੈ ਸੰਸਾਰੁ ॥ *He Himself is liberated, and He liberates the universe.* … ([Guru Granth Sahib - Sukhmani Sahib](https://api.banidb.com/))

```bilingual
ਆਪਿ ਮੁਕਤੁ ਮੁਕਤੁ ਕਰੈ ਸੰਸਾਰੁ ॥
*He Himself is liberated, and He liberates the universe.*<sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Banidb, [*Guru Granth Sahib - Sukhmani Sahib*](https://siftersearch.com/library/sikh/guru-granth-sahib/various-sikh-gurus_guru-granth-sahib-raag-asa)

When we examine the literature before us, different authorities and sources approach liberation in distinct ways. In the Buddhist tradition, the [*Sutra Collection (A, Part-2)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20937) records the Enlightening Being Universally Good entering into an inconceivable door of liberation, ["causing them all to be ultimately emancipated"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-2/?paraId=para_926&selectionString=buddhasutra_a_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bltm.0~buddhasutra_a_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bltm.1238) — *Sutra Collection (A, Part-2)*. In the [*Sutta Nipata*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20926), Siddhartha Buddha speaks of the individual realization where ["The man who knows in this world the destruction of his pain"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutta-nipata_buddha/?paraId=para_880&selectionString=suttanipata_en_r7.0~suttanipata_en_r7.109) is liberated, as found in [*The Sutta Nipata*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20926). Turning to the Sikh teachings in the [*Guru Granth Sahib*](https://siftersearch.com/library/sikh/guru-granth-sahib/various-sikh-gurus_guru-granth-sahib-raag-asa), Guru Nanak Dev Ji records that ["The faithful find the Door of Liberation"](https://api.banidb.com/) — [*Guru Granth Sahib - Japji Sahib*](https://siftersearch.com/library/sikh/guru-granth-sahib/various-sikh-gurus_guru-granth-sahib-raag-asa). In the records of early Bahá'í history, as recalled by Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab in [*‘Abdu’l-Bahá in Egypt*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt), ‘Abdu'l-Bahá remarks that ["Today the full realization of Universal Peace is a panacea for every social disease"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p515) — quoted in *‘Abdu’l-Bahá in Egypt* by Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab. Finally, the ancient Jain text the *Âkârâṅga Sûtra* simply opens the path toward ["Liberation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/akaranga-sutra/?paraId=para_226&selectionString=akaranga_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blgm.0~akaranga_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blgm.11) — *Âkârâṅga Sûtra*.

What these diverse passages share is the conviction that liberation—whether approached as a personal awakening from pain, a cosmic unfolding, or the establishment of peace—is the ultimate destination toward which the soul and the world are guided.

Warmly,
Anís

The speaker’s response to others is to share what they know with utmost kindness and goodwill, and if it is refused, to leave the person to himself and pray for his guidance.

We see this instruction clearly in the writings of Bahá’u’lláh: ["Consort with all men, O people of Bahá, in a spirit of friendliness and fellowship. If ye be aware of a certain truth, if ye possess a jewel, of which others are deprived, share it with them in a language of utmost kindliness and goodwill. If it be accepted, if it fulfill its purpose, your object is attained. When we look at how different levels of authority and commentary function across traditions, it helps to distinguish several layers. Authorized interpretation includes the specific explanations written by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Shoghi Effendi, which carry binding interpretive weight. Guidance from the Universal House of Justice provides administrative direction, legislation, and current institutional plans, but as established in its own mandate, it does not act as a doctrinal or interpretive authority. Beyond these, we find official exposition, historical scholarship, community practice, and individual synthesis or commentary—none of which carry the weight of scripture or authorized interpretation.

Warmly,

In the Bahá'í writings, Bahá’u’lláh addresses the divine origin of the human spirit and its intended relationship, asking, ["O Son of the Wondrous Vision! I have breathed within thee a breath of My own Spirit, that thou mayest be My lover."](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahaullah-and-the-new-era_john-esslemont/?paraId=para_383&selectionString=baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blcg.0~baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blcg.142) [*Bahá’u’lláh and the New Era*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20813), quoted in this work by John E. Esslemont. Similarly, in the Taoist tradition, Laozi points to this same orientation toward the enduring, stating simply that ["To know the eternal is to be enlightened."](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu) [*Tao Te Ching*](https://siftersearch.com/library/tao/foundational-classics/laozi-tr-gia-fu_tao-te-ching-tr-gia-fu-feng-and-jane-english).

These diverse expressions share a common recognition that when an individual awakens to the reality of the eternal within, life naturally aligns with a higher purpose of love, awareness, and transcendent realization.

Warmly,

Anís

Dear friend,

It is a quiet joy to look across traditions at how humans have turned to fasting, finding in hunger a way to clear the mirror of the heart. When we listen to the sources themselves, each voice reveals a distinct shape for this ancient practice, whether as bodily discipline, moral renewal, or an inward turning away from illusion.

Yet across the wider literature, such as [*The Mahabharata 13*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=912367), the question arises of how these vows are shared by all orders of people seeking merit and self-mastery.

In the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, the outward form of withholding food is constantly weighed against the inward reality of justice. The prophet Isaiah challenges those who ["fast for strife and debate"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-isaiah/?paraId=para_1045&selectionString=isaiah-ot_en_vo.0~isaiah-ot_en_vo.125) — [*The Bible (KJV)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=912528), reminding us that true observance cannot be separated from mercy toward others.

In Buddhist practice, days of abstinence like the *uposatha* are marked by deliberate restraint. As described in [*The Sutta Nipata*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20926), the believer keeps ["abstinence (uposatha) on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and the eighth days"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutta-nipata_buddha/?paraId=para_551&selectionString=suttanipata_en_i2.0~suttanipata_en_i2.176) — *The Sutta Nipata*, stepping back from ordinary appetites to examine the mind.

The Sufi master Ibn ‘Arabi writes in [*Selections from al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21081) that ["Fasting in reality is non-action, not action"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-al-futuhat-al-makkiyya_shaykh-muhyiddin-ibn/?paraId=para_506&selectionString=the_meccan_revelations_islam_ocean_en-blo2.0~the_meccan_revelations_islam_ocean_en-blo2.38) — *Selections from al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya*, pointing to a stillness where the self lets go of its constant grasping.

```
<sup>1</sup> Original Gurmukhi text from the Guru Granth Sahib (Sukhmani Sahib) · <sup>2</sup> English translation accessed via the Banidb API

Despite their differing calendars and rules, these traditions share a common movement: they all use the quiet discipline of the body to awaken a deeper attentiveness to the soul's true needs.

results.text: Best Bible Reading Order for Beginners

tmpl.reply:
Dear friend,

Approaching the Bible for the first time can feel like stepping into a vast library of many voices, histories, and songs. While readers often begin at the very beginning in Genesis, others find it helpful to start with the Gospels in the New Testament—such as the Gospel of Luke or the Gospel of John—to ground themselves in the narrative of Jesus before exploring the broader historical and prophetic books. The scriptures themselves encourage a deliberate and earnest approach to study, urging readers to seek understanding with an open heart: ["Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law."](https://oceanlibrary.com/book-of-psalms-tehilim_david/?paraId=para_2221&selectionString=psalms-ot_en_1se.0~psalms-ot_en_1se.57) — [*Psalms*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21243).

Because the Bible contains many different literary genres, readers often follow various sequences depending on what they hope to discover. Here is a short list of common reading approaches, though this list may be incomplete:

- **The Gospel-First Approach:** Starting with the New Testament Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) to understand the central figure of the tradition, followed by Acts and the Epistles.
- **The Chronological Approach:** Reading historical and prophetic books in the order the events are traditionally understood to have occurred, moving through the Hebrew Bible before the New Testament.
- **The Thematic Approach:** Weaving between the wisdom literature (like Psalms and Proverbs) and the narratives, allowing reflective prayers to accompany historical reading.

As you explore these writings, remember the advice found in the epistles regarding diligence in study: ["Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-second-epistle-to-timothy/?paraId=para_30&selectionString=the-second-epistle-to-timothy-nt_en_3j.0~the-second-epistle-to-timothy-nt_en_3j.98) — [*2 Timothy*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20971).

Warmly,
Anís

As Surendranath Dasgupta notes: ["Notwithstanding the radical differences in their philosophical notions Jainism and Buddhism, which were originally both orders of monks outside the pale of Brahmanism, present some resemblance in outward appearance..."](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/12956) — [*A History of Indian Philosophy Vol. 1*](https://siftersearch.com/library/hindu/philosophy/surendranath_a-history-of-indian-philosophy-vol-1).

The Buddhist tradition approaches the moral consequences of actions with a distinct understanding of ["the complexity of the kammic process, and its application of that understanding to the psychology of teaching."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-rs/?paraId=para_1451&selectionString=sutra_collection_rs_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6v.0~sutra_collection_rs_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6v.1002) — [*Sutra Collection (RS)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20937).

Hello again! I am so sorry the lines didn't come through clearly in my first note. Let's place them right in front of you so you and your study group can read them together.

To open with the passage about the Messengers' identity, we turn to [*The Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653) (revealed Scripture), where Bahá’u’lláh explains:

> ["It is clear and evident to thee that all the Prophets are the Temples of the Cause of God, Who have appeared clothed in divers attire. If thou wilt observe with discriminating eyes, thou wilt behold them all abiding in the same tabernacle, soaring in the same heaven, seated upon the same throne, uttering the same speech, and proclaiming the same Faith."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.1808) — *The Kitáb-i-Íqán*<sup>1</sup>

When we look at how this is understood across the various layers of the tradition, we see a clear distinction. Revealed Scripture provides the foundational text itself, such as this passage from Bahá’u’lláh. Authorized interpretation comes through the Guardian, Shoghi Effendi, who often drew directly upon these very words—as he did when writing:

> ["All the Prophets of God," asserts Bahá’u’lláh in the Kitáb-i-Íqán, "abide in the same tabernacle, soar in the same heaven, are seated upon the same throne, utter the same speech, and proclaim the same Faith."](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_166&selectionString=shoghi_effendi_world_order_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_en_76.0~shoghi_effendi_world_order_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_en_76.787) — [*The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20894)<sup>2</sup>

Beyond these, we have other categories: the Universal House of Justice provides legal authority and current administrative guidance for the community; official compilations (like [*Lights of Guidance*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20891), compiled by Helen Hornby) gather references together; scholarship, history, and community practice offer helpful context and study aids; and my own thoughts here are simply a personal synthesis of these texts. None of those latter categories establish doctrine or interpret scripture; only the original Writings and their authorized interpreters do that.

It is a profound thing to sit with a group and read these lines aloud, watching how the concept of "return" shifts from a literal repetition of a physical body to the reappearance of the eternal spirit and attributes of the Prophets in a new vessel. I hope this passage serves your group's discussion well.

Warmly,  
Anís

<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* · <sup>2</sup> Shoghi Effendi, *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*

>

When considering how this inner freedom relates to outward life, Shoghi Effendi writes in [*The Advent of Divine Justice*](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_73&selectionString=advent_of_divine_justice_v2_ocean_baha_i_en_4k.0~advent_of_divine_justice_v2_ocean_baha_i_en_4k.901) that moral conduct is "not to be associated or confused with any form of asceticism, or of excessive and bigoted puritanism," noting that Bahá’u’lláh's standard "seeks, under no circumstances, to deny anyone the legitimate right and privilege to derive the fullest advantage and benefit from the manifold joys, beauties, and pleasures with which the world has been so plentifully enriched by an All-Loving Creator."

Similarly, a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi (quoted in the [*Compilation for the 2018 Counsellors’ Conference*](https://oceanlibrary.com/compilation-for-the-2018-counsellors-conference_bahaullah/?paraId=para_39&selectionString=give_me_thy_grace_to_serve_thy_loved_ones_ocean_en-bl3e.0~give_me_thy_grace_to_signer_en-bl3e.610)) points out that dividing one's time between serving the Faith and attending to other duties "is a compromise between the two verses of the 'Aqdas', one making it incumbent upon every Bahá’í to serve the promotion of the Faith and the other that every soul should be occupied in some form of occupation that will benefit society." ([Compilation for the 2018 Counsellors’ Conference](https://oceanlibrary.com/compilation-for-the-2018-counsellors-conference_bahaullah/?paraId=para_39&selectionString=give_me_thy_grace_to_serve_thy_loved_ones_ocean_en-bl3e.0~give_me_thy_grace_to_serve_thy_loved_ones_ocean_en-bl3e.610))

It is striking to see how the texts ask for an absolute reorientation of the heart—surrendering attachment to one's own existence and worldly vanities—while simultaneously requiring daily labor, lawful work, and the enjoyment of the world's blessings. Detachment appears to be a condition of the spirit rather than a rejection of life's practical duties.

Warmly,
Anís

tmpl.reply:
Dear friend,

Do all religions teach the soul? Not in the same way, for while traditions frequently speak of an enduring inner reality or an invisible self, they often mean entirely different things by it.

Where some traditions trace a permanent spiritual essence, others—such as Buddhism—approach the person through teachings of non-self, noting in the [*Sutra Collection (A, Part-1)*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1/?paraId=para_459&selectionString=budhist_sutra_part_a_ocean_buddhism_en-blf8.0~budhist_sutra_part_a_ocean_buddhism_en-blf8.33) how people ask whether ["‘The soul and the body are the same’"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1/?paraId=para_459&selectionString=budhist_sutra_part_a_ocean_buddhism_en-blf8.0~budhist_sutra_part_a_ocean_buddhism_en-blf8.33) while exploring the dissolution of fixed identities. By contrast, Hindu texts view this reality as transcendent over physical forms, described in the [*Svetāsvatara Upanishad*](https://oceanlibrary.com/svetasvatara-upanishad/?paraId=para_96&selectionString=svetasvatara_upanishad_ocean_en_5k.0~svetasvatara_upanishad_ocean_en_5k.83) as something that is ["whatever body it takes, with that it is joined"](https://oceanlibrary.com/svetasvatara-upanishad/?paraId=para_96&selectionString=svetasvatara_upanishad_ocean_en_5k.0~svetasvatara_upanishad_ocean_en_5k.83). In Islamic thought, al-Ghazálí portrays the soul in his [*Revival of Religious Learnings Vol-IV*](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali/?paraId=para_1403&selectionString=the_revival_of_religious_learning_vol4_islam_ocean50a36bcc2251e1182f42f2dfde95a466-bl5tl.0~the_revival_of_religious_learning_vol4_islam_ocean50a36bcc2251e1182f42f2dfde95a466-bl5tl.33) as a subtle, reflective substance—noting elsewhere in [*Revival of Religious Learnings Vol-III*](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-3_imam-ghazzali/?paraId=para_42&selectionString=revival_of_religious_sciences_v_3_ocean_islam_en-bl4d.0~revival_of_religious_sciences_v_3_ocean_islam_en-bl4d.509) that ["the soul of a believer is bright and there is a bright lamp in it"](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-3_imam-ghazzali/?paraId=para_42&selectionString=revival_of_religious_sciences_v_3_ocean_islam_en-bl4d.0~revival_of_religious_sciences_v_3_ocean_islam_en-bl4d.509). Zoroastrian liturgy similarly preserves the memory and reality of ["the soul of the righteous"](https://oceanlibrary.com/yashts/?paraId=fn_1362), while Jewish mystical tradition explores ["the highest form of the soul"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kabbalah-neerav_moses-ben-jacob-cordovero/?paraId=fn_246) within Kabbalah, as Moses ben Jacob Cordovero notes. In the Bahá'í writings, Bahá'u'lláh describes this reality directly, explaining in the [*Tablet on the Right of the People*](https://bahai-library.com/brown_lawh_haqqu_nas) that ["Each human being has an essence and reality - that is, the soul - and our deeds are its attributes"](https://bahai-library.com/brown_lawh_haqqu_nas).

It is a quiet wonder to watch how different windows let in the light, each naming the unseen center of human life in its own language.

Warmly,
Anís

results.text: How do I let go of my anxiety about death and about the meaning of life?

tmpl.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a very human thing to look at the boundaries of our days and wonder what holds them together, or what waits when they close. The weight of that question can feel heavy to carry alone, but the voices left to us across the traditions suggest we are not the first to stand facing it.

When Confucius was asked about the unseen transition of death, he turned the question back toward the ground beneath our feet, answering in [*The Analects*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20997): ["Where there is scarcely the ability to minister to living men, how shall there be ability to minister to the spirits?” On his venturing to put a question concerning death, he answered, “Where there is scarcely any knowledge about life, how shall there be any about death?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius/?paraId=para_429&selectionString=theanalects_ocean_confucius_en-blgd.0~theanalects_ocean_confucius_en-blgd.311) — *The Analects*. There is a steadying simplicity in that: perhaps the meaning we search for in the abstract is meant to be found right here, in how we inhabit the breath we have.

Yet when the dread of death itself presses close, the texts offer different ways of looking right at it. In the Buddhist tradition, the [*Sutta Nipata*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20926) speaks of a quiet fearlessness born from letting go of the internal storms that bind us: ["Having abandoned both passion and hatred and folly, having rent the ties, not trembling in the loss of life, let one wander alone like a rhinoceros."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutta-nipata_buddha/?paraId=para_82&selectionString=suttanipata_en_51.0~suttanipata_en_51.123) — [*The Sutta Nipata*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20926). And in the Psalms, the shadow of that final transition loses its terror not because the path is easy, but because of companionship: ["Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."](https://oceanlibrary.com/book-of-psalms-tehilim_david/?paraId=para_351&selectionString=psalms-ot_en_cg.0~psalms-ot_en_cg.114) — [*The Bible (KJV), Psalms*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=912528).

The Sikh tradition, too, looks directly at the breaking of that fear through absorption in something larger than our passing days. Guru Arjan Dev Ji writes in the [*Guru Granth Sahib*](https://siftersearch.com/library/sikh/guru-granth-sahib/various-sikh-gurus_guru-granth-sahib-raag-asa) of how the root of mortal anxiety is undone:

> ਸੰਤ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਤੇ ਜਮ ਤੇ ਛੁਟੈ ॥ *By the Grace of the Saint, one escapes the Messenger of Death.* … ([Guru Granth Sahib - Sukhmani Sahib](https://api.banidb.com/))

```bilingual
ਹਰਿ ਜਨ ਹਰਿ ਹਰਿ ਨਾਮਿ ਸਮਾਣੇ ਦੁਖੁ ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭਵ ਖੰਡਾ ਹੇ ॥
The humble servants of the Lord are absorbed in the Name of the Lord, Har, Har. The pain of birth and the fear of death are eradicated.<sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation from Guru Granth Sahib (Sikh scripture)

To let go of anxiety may not mean finding an intellectual answer that solves the unknown, but rather shifting where we place our weight—moving from the terror of what ends to the reality of what sustains us right now.

Warmly,
Anís

results.text: what are you?
Bahá'u'lláh was imprisoned in the Síyáh-Chál (Black Pit) of Tehran in 1852 — the moment of his revelation. What happened in that pit, and why does it matter that revelation came in such conditions?

tmpl.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a striking thing to consider that the year 1269 A.H.—foreshadowed by the Báb as the "Year Nine"—began on October 15, 1852, right at the midpoint of Bahá'u'lláh’s four-month imprisonment in the Síyáh-Chál, the dark, foul-smelling, subterranean dungeon in Ṭihrán ([*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20901) ([Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-extracts-and-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=fn_15)), [*The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307) ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah))).

As recorded in the sources, it was in the midst of this darkness and agony that Bahá'u'lláh received His Prophetic Mission (*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks* ([Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-extracts-and-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=fn_15))). He Himself described the experience during those infrequent moments of slumber when the galling weight of the chains and the stench-filled air allowed Him little rest:

> During the days I lay in the prison of Ṭihrán, though the galling weight of the chains and the stench-filled air allowed Me but little sleep, still in those infrequent moments of slumber I felt as if something flowed from the crown of My head over My breast, even as a mighty torrent that precipitateth itself upon the earth from the summit of a lofty mountain. Every limb of My body would, as a result, be set afire. At such … ([*Revelation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20986) ([Revelation](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-apocalypse-saint-john-of-patmos)) by Adib Taherzadeh, quoting Bahá'u'lláh)

Shoghi Effendi notes that under the impact of this experience, Bahá'u'lláh felt the onrushing force of His newly revealed Mission flowing like a mighty torrent ([*Citadel of Faith. Messages to America 1947-1957*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20882) ([Citadel of Faith. Messages to America 1947-1957](https://oceanlibrary.com/citadel-of-faith_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_535&selectionString=citadel_of_faith_messages_to_america_1947_1957_en-blhm.0~citadel_of_faith_messages_to_america_1947_1957_en-blhm.829))). In that same vision, the "Most Great Spirit" appeared to Him in the guise of a "Maiden" calling with a wondrous, sweet voice (*Citadel of Faith. Messages to America 1947-1957* ([Citadel of Faith. Messages to America 1947-1957](https://oceanlibrary.com/citadel-of-faith_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_535&selectionString=citadel_of_faith_messages_to_america_1947_1957_en-blhm.0~citadel_of_faith_messages_to_america_1947_1957_en-blhm.829))). It is also generally believed that His earliest extant revelation, the Persian poem known as [*Rashh-i Amá*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/books/bahaullah_rashh-i-ama-les-nuees-du-plus-haut-des-cieux) (the [*Tablet of the Mist of the Unknown*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-the-mist-of-the-unknown)), was revealed during these months in the dungeon (*Tablet of the Mist of the Unknown* ([Tablet of the Mist of the Unknown](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_rashh_ama_neshati))).

There is a profound wonder in this contrast: that a revelation intended to reshape the spiritual life of humanity should be born not in halls of comfort or outward power, but in the depths of a subterranean pit, amidst chains and oppression. It suggests that spiritual force arises entirely from within, independent of material conditions, proving that outer darkness cannot stifle the dawning of an inner light.

Warmly,

Anís

none.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a striking thing that the birth-hour of a world faith should be sought in a subterranean dungeon—the Síyáh-Chál, or Black Pit, of Tehran—during the autumn of 1852. As ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes, the Islamic year 1269 opened precisely at the midpoint of that four-month imprisonment, a date foreseen by the Báb as the "Year Nine" ([*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20901)).

Within that dark, foul-smelling enclosure ([*The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307)), weighed down by heavy chains amid pestilential air ([*Revelation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20986) quoted in *The Apocalypse of Saint John*), the conditions were as far removed from worldly power as a place could be. Yet it was precisely there that Bahá’u’lláh received His Prophetic Mission (*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*).

Bahá’u’lláh Himself described how the experience of revelation came to Him in those infrequent moments when sleep overcame the torment of the dungeon. His own words, preserved in His writings, offer a rare window into that inward event:

> During the days I lay in the prison of Ṭihrán, though the galling weight of the chains and the stench-filled air allowed Me but little sleep, still in those infrequent moments of slumber I felt as if something flowed from the crown of My head over My breast, even as a mighty torrent that precipitateth itself upon the earth from the summit of a lofty mountain. Every limb of My body would, as a result, be set afire. At such … (*Revelation* quoted in *The Apocalypse of Saint John*)

Shoghi Effendi notes how there, under the impact of a vision, the Most Great Spirit appeared to Him as a Maiden calling with a wondrous voice, and the onrushing force of His newly revealed Mission flowed through Him ([*Citadel of Faith*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=341125)). Out of these depths also emerged His earliest extant revelation composed in Iran, the Persian poem known as [*Rashh-i Ama*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/books/bahaullah_rashh-i-ama-les-nuees-du-plus-haut-des-cieux) ([*Tablet of the Mist of the Unknown*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-the-mist-of-the-unknown)).

Why revelation should come in such conditions is a quiet question at the heart of how spiritual order enters the world. When outward force seeks to extinguish a cause by casting its bearer into darkness and chains, the source of authority proves to be entirely independent of material circumstances. The contrast between the absolute power of the jailers above and the sovereign, unvanquished spirit waking in the pit below suggests that divine order does not lean upon human dominion or comfort. It rises, instead, from a source untouched by them.

Warmly,  
Anís

results.text: What do Islamic teachings emphasize about showing honor and deference to one's mother and father?

tmpl.reply:
Greetings, friend.

Islamic teachings place a profound emphasis on honoring and deferring to one's parents, linking this duty directly to the worship of God. In the Qur'an, kindness to parents is commanded immediately after the injunction to worship God alone, framing filial respect as a fundamental spiritual obligation.

The texts record specific guidance on how this honor should be expressed in daily life, especially as parents age. Believers are instructed to avoid even the smallest expressions of impatience or disrespect. As rendered in [*The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr/?paraId=para_2331&selectionString=the_holy_quran_tr_by_yusuf_ali_islam_ocean_en-bl2kz.0~the_holy_quran_tr_by_yusuf_ali_islam_ocean_en-bl2kz.182):

> Whether one
> Or both of them attain
> Old age in thy life,
> Say not to them a word
> Of contempt, nor repel them,
> But address them
> In terms of honour.

This call for tenderness is mirrored in [*The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XVII. The Night Journey*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xvii-the-night-journey_muhammad/?paraId=para_12&selectionString=sura_xvii_the_night_journey_quran_ocean_en-bl1on.0~sura_xvii_the_night_journey_quran_ocean_en-bl1on.399), which urges children to "defer humbly to them out of tenderness" and to pray for them with the same care they received in childhood: “Lord, have compassion on them both, even as they reared me when I was little.”

The tradition also highlights the immense physical and emotional labor of motherhood, noting the pain of bearing, bringing forth, and weaning a child (*[The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XLVI. Al Ahkaf](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xlvi-al-ahkaf_muhammad/?paraId=para_12&selectionString=sura_xlvi_al_ahkaf_quran_ocean_en-bl3om.0~sura_xlvi_al_ahkaf_quran_ocean_en-bl3om.405)*). Perhaps because of this foundational sacrifice, the Prophet Muhammad emphasized the mother's unique claim on a child's reverence. In a recorded encounter from [*Kitab Al-Kafi 2*](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-al-kafi-2/?paraId=para_2064&selectionString=kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl238.0~kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl238.232) by Al-Kulayni, when a man asked about kindness to parents, the Prophet replied: “Be kind to your mother, be kind to your mother, be kind to your mother, be kind to your father, be kind to your father, and be kind to your father. He began with mother before the father.”

At the same time, this respect has a defined boundary. If parents attempt to pressure a believer into associating other deities with God or acting without knowledge, obedience to them on that specific point is withheld, though kindness in daily companionship is still maintained (*[The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XXIX. The Spider](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xxix-the-spider_muhammad/?paraId=para_6&selectionString=sura_xxviii_the_story_quran_ocean_en-bl2q1.0~sura_xxviii_the_story_quran_ocean_en-bl2q1.299)*).

It is remarkable how consistently these texts ask us to look back at the fragility of our own beginnings—and to meet the vulnerability of our parents with deep, active grace.

Warmly,  
Anís

Surendranath Dasgupta notes that this ["principle of extreme carefulness not to destroy any living being has been in monastic life carried out to its very last consequences"](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/12956) [*A History of Indian Philosophy Vol. 1*](https://siftersearch.com/library/hindu/philosophy/surendranath_a-history-of-indian-philosophy-vol-1).

It is a striking thing to witness a human being moving through the world with such acute tenderness toward the unseen life beneath their feet. While different traditions approach this care in their own ways—such as the Hindu injunction of ["heed to injure nought which lives"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita/?paraId=para_231&selectionString=bhagavad-gita_en_9b.0~bhagavad-gita_en_9b.599) found in [*The Bhagavad-Gita*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21038)—the Jain monastic practice makes that inner reverence an entirely visible, physical act of clearing the way before every step.

If you would like to explore further, we might look into the specific vows of monks and nuns in Jain texts or examine how other traditions view non-harming (*ahimsa*).

Warmly,  
Anís

Every community must continually decide how its foundational principles apply to the shifting customs around it.

Warmly,
Anís
